SARDAR MUHAMMAD SARFRAZ DOGAR CJ:- Through the instant petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, (“the Constitution”), the petitioner, a resident and businessman of Islamabad, has invoked the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court principally on the apprehension of disruption of civic life in the Islamabad Capital W.P No.4421 of 2026 4 Territory on account of a proposed political long march announced by the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (“PTI”) for 27.09.2026.

2. The petitioner states in his petition that he is engaged in the business under the name and style of “Friends Heavy Machinery” and depends upon uninterrupted access to roads, highways and the general civic infrastructure of the Federal Capital for carrying on his trade and meeting financial and commercial obligations. According to him, the proposed long march is not a speculative apprehension, inasmuch as its date has allegedly been publicly announced, reiterated by the political leadership of PTI, and, according to the material placed on record, the Chief Minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has stated that he would himself lead the march.

3. The petition refers, inter alia, to statements allegedly made on 05.08.2026, 10.08.2026 and 23.08.2026, whereby the date and proposed character of the march were reiterated. The petitioner has further relied upon newspaper reports, official correspondence and material relating to earlier political protests, particularly the events of 2014, May 2022 and November 2024, to contend that large-scale political gatherings entering Islamabad have previously resulted in closure or obstruction of roads, disruption of traffic, impediment to emergency services and damage to public and private property.

4. It has been pleaded that the petitioner and other citizens of Islamabad apprehend interference with their fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 9, 14, 15, 18, 23, 24 and 25 of the Constitution, particularly the rights to movement, dignity, lawful W.P No.4421 of 2026 5 trade and business, and enjoyment of property. The petitioner also invokes Articles 16, 17 and 19 of the Constitution, not in denial of the right of peaceful political assembly and expression, but on the footing that such rights are subject to reasonable restrictions and cannot lawfully be exercised in a manner which disables the rest of the citizenry from using public roads, accessing hospitals, attending courts and workplaces, or carrying on ordinary civic and commercial life. The petitioner has sought this Court’s intervention to ensure the enforcement of his fundamental rights. The petitioner also invokes the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, 2024, contending that the proposed assembly cannot lawfully take place in Islamabad except in accordance with the statutory regime. The petitioner seeks, in substance, preventive directions to the Federal Government, Islamabad Capital Territory Administration, lawenforcement agencies and the Governments and police authorities of the Provinces to ensure that public roads and emergency corridors are not unlawfully occupied or obstructed and that official vehicles, police personnel, public funds, governmental machinery and other state resources are not utilized for partisan political mobilisation.

5. It is further alleged that the use of provincial governmental machinery for political mobilisation, particularly by the sitting Chief Minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, would offend the constitutional obligation of the State to act impartially and to protect the fundamental rights of other citizens. Reliance has also been placed on the Rules of Business, 1973, the Police Order, 2002 and other governmental arrangements to demonstrate a W.P No.4421 of 2026 6 federal nexus in relation to officers, police personnel and official resources.

6. The petitioner consequently seeks, inter alia, declarations against unlawful occupation or obstruction of public roads and directions to the concerned authorities to take all lawful and proportionate preventive measures so that the proposed procession does not interfere with the ordinary functioning of the Federal Capital. A further prayer has been made for restraining the use of governmental machinery, public funds, official vehicles, police resources and other state resources for political mobilisation.

7. Given the importance of the questions emanating from the instant Petition, notice under Order XXVII-A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (“CPC”) was issued to the learned Attorney-General for Pakistan, who addressed this Court on all issues, at length. Separately, notices were also issued to the learned Advocate Generals of all Provinces as well as to Islamabad Capital Territory (“ICT”) to present their respective Governments including Chief Ministers of all the Provinces and ICT.

8. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the petition raises issues directly touching upon enforcement of fundamental rights and the constitutional responsibility of the State to protect citizens before rather than after an avoidable breakdown of public order. He submitted that Articles 15, 18, 23 and 24 protect not merely abstract liberties but the practical ability of citizens to move, work, carry on lawful business and enjoy their property. Learned counsel placed particular reliance W.P No.4421 of 2026 7 upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Suo Motu Case No.7 of 2017, PLD 2019 SC 318 (Faizabad Dharna Case), submitting that the right to protest, although constitutionally protected, is not absolute and remains subject to the rights of other citizens and to reasonable regulation in the interest of public order. It was argued that the State cannot remain passive until roads are blocked, businesses paralysed, emergency services impeded and public or private property damaged.

9. Learned counsel further referred to “Islamabad High Court Bar Association v. Federation of Pakistan”, (PLD 2022 SC 511), and other constitutional authorities concerning movement, public order and political protest, and argued that the proposed march, in the circumstances pleaded, presents sufficiently concrete and imminent apprehension to justify preventive judicial intervention.

10. As regards jurisdiction, learned counsel submitted that Article 199(1)(c) deliberately employs the expression “any person or authority, including any Government” and extends the jurisdiction to a Government “exercising any power or performing any function in, or in relation to, any territory within the jurisdiction of that Court.” According to learned counsel, therefore, the fact that certain respondents belong to the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa or other Provincial Governments does not, by itself, oust the jurisdiction of this Court where their acts or functions have a direct bearing upon the threatened infringement of fundamental rights within Islamabad. W.P No.4421 of 2026 8 11. Learned counsel emphasized the public character of the controversy and submitted that the relief sought is preventive, neutral and directed towards preservation of constitutional rights rather than suppression of any political activity. He maintained that no political party, however powerful, possesses an indefeasible right to occupy or block public roads or to employ state resources for partisan purposes. Learned counsel for the petitioner prayed for the acceptance of instant writ petition in terms of the relief sought therein.

12. Learned Attorney-General for Pakistan, while relying upon the orders and directions issued by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the Suo Motu case No.7/Faizabad Dharna Case (PLD 2019 SC 318) submitted that the State is under a positive constitutional duty to protect the fundamental rights of citizens and to ensure that political protest does not degenerate into an obstruction of civic life.

13. Learned Attorney-General further submitted that Article 199(1)(c) is couched in sufficiently broad terms to empower a High Court, in appropriate circumstances, to issue directions to a Government where its functions are being performed “in, or in relation to” the territory falling within the jurisdiction of that Court. It was consequently argued that the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court is not barred particularly where the proposed activity is directed towards entering Islamabad and allegedly affecting the rights of persons within the Federal Capital.

14. According to learned Attorney-General, the constitutional question cannot be approached by compartmentalizing W.P No.4421 of 2026 9 governmental responsibility into provincial territorial silos where the threatened infringement is itself trans-provincial in character. The State, he argued, must act cohesively to ensure protection of the constitutional rights of citizens within Islamabad.

15. Learned Advocate Generals Sindh, Punjab and Balochistan, while somehow reiterating the grounds mentioned in the petition, expressed no objection upon the issuance of any directions from this Court. Most importantly, they also did not object to the jurisdiction of this Court in that respect.

16. Conversely, Learned Advocate-General, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, vehemently opposed the petition. While referring to the Article 199 of the Constitution, his principal objection was to the assumption of jurisdiction by this Court over the Government and police authorities of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He submitted that the respondents against whom substantive directions are sought are provincial authorities functioning outside the territorial jurisdiction of this Court and that Article 199 does not confer upon a High Court general supervisory jurisdiction over the administration of another Province.

17. Learned Advocate-General further objected to the petition on the ground of non-joinder of the Chief Minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, particularly when the principal factual premise of the petition is that the Chief Minister himself intends to lead the proposed political march. According to him, no adverse declaration or restraint touching upon the Chief Minister could lawfully be issued in his absence. He also argued that the petition is premature and that the petitioner has an adequate statutory mechanism under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, W.P No.4421 of 2026 10 2024. He referred in particular to section 5 of the Act, contending that the District Magistrate possesses the statutory authority to prohibit an assembly where the prescribed conditions exist. It was submitted that the Court should not bypass the statutory scheme and assume the role assigned by legislature to the District Magistrate and the other authorities constituted under the said Act. He further argued that the petitioner has alternate remedy to approach to District Magistrate and against the decision of District Magistrate, he can resort to file Appeal or Revision as provided under section 6 of Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, 2024, therefore, instant constitutional petition is not maintainable. It was, therefore, urged that the petition be dismissed on the grounds of want of territorial jurisdiction, nonjoinder of a necessary party and availability of an adequate alternative statutory remedy.

18. In addition to above, learned Advocate General KPK argued that the proposed march is peaceful, which is fundamental right of every citizen or political party. He emphasized that this right is constitutionally recognized, which the petitioner has no locus standi to challenge.

19. Learned Advocate General, ICT argued vehemently in support of instant petition. He submitted that although learned Advocate General, KPK has stated at bar that proposed march would be peaceful and for democratic purport, however, the statements of PTI’s leadership particularly of KPK, express that it is intended for the purpose of release of a convict and to derail and oust the Government. He argued that both the purposes are illegal and unconstitutional as a convict can only be released by W.P No.4421 of 2026 11 the order of Courts in accordance with law and there is also a mechanism to oust the present regime of Government. These objectives cannot be lawfully achieved by sit-ins/Rallies or Dharnas. Learned Advocate General, argued that there is no doubt that there are constitutional rights under articles 15, 16 & 17, however, those are conditional and subject to restrictions. Therefore, cannot be allowed to be exercised to infringe the rights of other citizens. He also laid emphasis on sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, 2024. Lastly, he argued that if the proposed strength of the protesters, as allegedly announced by the political party i.e. in millions, are brought to Islamabad, the Administration of ICT would be unable to tackle the armed marchers being escorted by the provincial state machinery/resources. He also submitted that ICT Police does not have the capacity to tackle such large number of armed protesters. Lastly, he urged for issuing the appropriate directions.

20. We have heard learned counsels for the petitioner, learned Attorney General for Pakistan, learned Advocate Generals for Punjab, Sindh, KPK, Balochistan and Islamabad, at length and have perused the relevant record with their able assistance.

21. The controversy before us requires an unusual degree of constitutional balance. On one side stands the right of citizens and political parties to assemble peacefully, express political dissent and participate in democratic activity; on the other stand the equally constitutional rights of the wider citizenry to life, liberty, dignity, free movement, lawful trade and business, property, access to hospitals, educational institutions, courts and W.P No.4421 of 2026 12 workplaces, and to the continued functioning of the Federal Capital as the seat of the constitutional organs of the State. Therefore, the question is not whether a political party is entitled to protest. It plainly is, subject always to the Constitution and law, to what extent can this Court intervene before the event; and whether Article 199(1)(c) permits a High Court to issue directions to governmental authorities situated in another Province where the challenged governmental function has a direct nexus with the territory and fundamental rights falling within that High Court's jurisdiction. To address this question, constitutional scheme is of much significance.

15. Freedom of movement, etc. Every citizen shall have the right to remain in, and, subject to any reasonable restriction imposed by law in the public interest, enter and move freely throughout Pakistan and to reside and settle in any part thereof.
16. Freedom of assembly. Every citizen shall have the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of public order.

17. Freedom of association. (1) Every citizen shall have the right to form associations or unions, subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of sovereignty or integrity of Pakistan, public order or morality.

(2) Every citizen, not being in the service of Pakistan, shall have the right to form or be a member of a political party, subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of the sovereignty or integrity of Pakistan and such law shall provide that where the Federal Government declares that any political party has been formed or is operating in a manner prejudicial to the sovereignty or integrity of Pakistan, the Federal Government shall, within fifteen days of such declaration, refer the matter to the Federal Constitutional Court of Pakistan whose decision on such reference shall be final.
(3) Every political party shall account for the source of its funds in accordance with law.

The enjoyment of all above said rights has been made condition upon subject to any reasonable restriction imposed by law in the W.P No.4421 of 2026 13 public interest, subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of public order, and subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of sovereignty or integrity of Pakistan, public order or morality, respectively. There are four important components for enjoyment of these rights:
1. Assembly must be peaceful.
2. It must be without arms.
3. Restrictions must be imposed by law.
4. Restrictions must be reasonable and connected with public order.

These rights are consequently fundamental but not absolute. The right to protest, association and peaceful assembly and imposition of reasonable restrictions in this regard are discussed by the superior courts in a number of case laws.

22. In case titled as “Shuhada Forum Balochistan v. Justice (R) Jawad S.Khawaja” (P L D 2025 Supreme Court 482), it has been held that “all fundamental rights enshrined and envisaged under the Constitution are subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the law. Peaceful assembly, association, or public demonstration/ protest within the bounds and precincts of reasonable restrictions imposed by the law is not prohibited but without violating or breaking the law, or taking the law in one's hands”. In case titled as “Alamgir Khan vs. The State, etc.,” (2020 S C M R 759), it has been held that:- “…Freedom of speech is a most cherished right, guaranteed under the Constitution; it is certainly subject to "reasonable restrictions" within the contemplation of Article 19 thereof; whether in his outburst, mentioned in the transcript, the petitioner contravened the stipulated restrictions, is a question to be best settled by the trial Court, having regard to the totality of the impugned discourse, after conclusion of evidence. State must be benign upon dissent and criticism of its citizens, no matter how crudely articulated or misplaced, on the issues of desecration of the right to life during war W.P No.4421 of 2026 14 through opinions, though subjective, nonetheless, actuated by personal anguish; it must stand on surer foundations…”
(Emphasis supplied)

The hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in authoritative judgment rendered in Suo Motu Case No.7 of 2017 (P L D 2019 Supreme Court 318) has discussed the subject matter in detail. The relevant paragraphs are hereby reproduced for ready reference:- 12. Preventing the sick from reaching doctors and hospitals infringes their right to life (guaranteed under Article 9 of the Constitution) which requires enforcement. Blocking roads for long durations prevents citizens from exercising their right to freedom of movement (guaranteed by Article 15 of the Constitution) and this right of theirs requires enforcement. When students cannot attend schools and educational institutions their right to education (guaranteed under Article 25A of the Constitution) requires enforcement. When litigants' access to courts is blocked their right to fair trial and due process (guaranteed by Article 10A of the Constitution) requires enforcement. Abusing, threatening and attacking people undermines their right to live a life of "dignity" (guaranteed under Article 14 (1) of the Constitution) which requires enforcement. When shops and businesses are forced to shut, when people cannot pursue their vocation, when poor daily workers are denied the possibility of earning a livelihood their right to work (guaranteed by Article 18 of the Constitution) requires enforcement. When property is damaged or destroyed the right to hold and enjoy property (guaranteed under Article 23 of the Constitution) requires enforcement.

The Right to Protest 25. The Constitution does not specifically stipulate a right to protest. However, democracy recognizes such a right, and it was through democratic means that Pakistan was achieved. The people of the subcontinent acquired independence from British-colonial rule by the efforts of the All India Muslim League and the Indian National Congress; they peacefully protested, demonstrated, held meetings and expressed themselves through elections, as a consequence of which two independent countries, Pakistan and India, emerged. Our Constitution is moored in democracy. The people of Pakistan have declared, "that Pakistan would be a democratic State" and that its citizens are, "dedicated to the preservation of democracy". Citizens have the right to peacefully protest and hold demonstrations, and may do so against any action or decision of a government or authority. The W.P No.4421 of 2026 15 right to protest is also implied in "the right to assemble peacefully", in the "right to form associations or unions", in the "right to form or be a member of a political party" and in the "in the right to freedom of speech and expression".

The Right to Assemble Peacefully 27. The "right to assemble peacefully and without arms" is "subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of public order". The right of assembly is recognized as a right to preserve the democratic order, but it cannot be used to overthrow a lawful government. Nor can the right of assembly be used to bring about a revolution or insurrection. These principles were enunciated in the case of Islamic Republic of Pakistan v Abdul Wali Khan:

It goes without saying that while the right of Assembly is a very important right for the preservation of a democratic political system yet it cannot be denied that no State can tolerate utterances or actions which threaten to overthrow the Government established by law in that State by unlawful or unconstitutional means. As observed by the American Supreme Court in the case of American Communications v. Douds [(1951) 340 US 268], 'Freedom of speech, press and Assembly are dependent upon the power of the constitutional Government to survive. If it is to survive, it must have the power to protect itself against unlawful conduct and, under some circumstance, against incitements to commit unlawful acts'.

The maintenance of public order is the paramount duty of the State. If anyone propagates, "hatred or contempt, or excites or attempts to excite disaffection towards the Federal or Provincial Government" they commit the offence of sedition for which the punishment is imprisonment for life.”
(Emphasis supplied)

In case titled as “PAKISTAN BROADCASTERS ASSOCIATION and others v. PAKISTAN ELECTRONIC MEDIA REGULATORY AUTHORITY and others” (PLD 2016 Supreme Court 692), it was held as under:- “…Undoubtedly no one can be deprived of his fundamental rights. Such rights being incapable of being divested or abridged. The W.P No.4421 of 2026 16 legislative powers conferred on the State functionaries can be exercised only to regulate these rights through reasonable restrictions, and that too only as may be mandated by law and not otherwise. The authority wielding statutory powers conferred on it must act reasonably (emphasis supplied) and within the scope of the powers so conferred… …However, in examining the reasonableness of any restriction on the right to freedom of expression it also should essentially be kept in mind as to whether in purporting to exercise freedom of expression one is infringing upon the aforesaid right of others, and also violating their right to live a nuisance free life, as to whether one's right to time and space is being violated. It should also be kept in mind that none can be forced to listen or watch that he may not like to, and that one cannot be invaded with unsolicited interruptions while eagerly watching or listening to something of his interest. The State is not supposed to remain oblivious of such violation/invasions and cannot detract from its obligation to regulate the right to speech when it comes in conflict with the right of the viewers or listeners. It was perhaps keeping in view, inter alia, the foregoing that the framers of our Constitution, though secured the right to free speech, but have not left the same unchecked, and have provided for reasonable restriction as postulated under Article 19 of the Constitution. Indeed the State has a compelling interest in regulating the right to speech when it comes in conflict with the rights of other individuals, or other societal interests.

…It is indeed true that freedom of expression being a natural fundamental right cannot be suppressed unless the same is being exploited and/or is causing danger to, or in it lies the imminent potential of hurting public interest, or putting it at stake directly, and also that the anticipated danger should not be remote, conjectural or far fetched. It should rather have proximate and direct nexus with the expression.

…However it may be kept in mind that in a civilized and democratic society, restrictions and duties co-exist in order to protect and preserve the right to speech, it is inevitable to maintain equilibrium, and for that to place reasonable restriction on this freedom in the maintenance of “public order” and unless the restriction strikes a proper balance between the freedom guaranteed by Article 19 of the Constitution and the social control permitted thereby, it must be held to lack the attributes of reasonableness…”
(Emphasis supplied)

W.P No.4421 of 2026 17 In “Raja Hassan AkhtarVs. Federation of Pakistan etc.,” (W.P. No.2974/2024), this Court passed the order dated 05.10.2024, wherein it was held that:- “It is pertinent to note at this juncture that under Articles 16 and 17 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, the freedoms of assembly and movement are fundamental rights provided to the citizens of Pakistan, however are subject to reasonable and proportional restrictions in accordance with law. Such restrictions are only justifiable through a legitimate purpose which must be in the best interest of the larger public. Maintenance of peace and law and order in Islamabad Capital Territory is the responsibility of the Ministry of Interior and ICT Administration. However, while performing their duties and functions, the principles of proportionality and legitimacy of public purpose and aim bind the said authorities and prevent harsh or disproportionate restrictions which would otherwise amount to unlawful infringement of rights.”
(Emphasis supplied)

In case titled “RIAZ HANIF RAHI v. Federation of Pakistan and others” (P L D 2020 Islamabad 175), this Court held as follows:- “4. It is noted that peaceful protest by unarmed persons is a constitutionally protected right. This right stems from the fundamental rights of freedom of assembly, freedom of association and freedom of speech/expression, which are guaranteed under Articles 16, 17 and 19 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, respectively. No law-abiding citizen can, therefore, be denied the right of peaceful protest. However, correspondingly the peaceful protesters cannot be allowed to infringe the fundamental rights of other citizens. It is thus the duty of public functionaries to ensure that the constitutionally guaranteed rights of every citizen are protected. Maintaining public order is a crucial responsibility of the State and its functionaries. The right to protest is indeed not an absolute right but it is subject to reasonable restrictions. It is the responsibility of the law enforcing authorities to consider several factors while imposing restrictions or conditions for the purposes of regulating a peaceful protest so that the rights of other citizens also remain protected. In this regard they may impose restrictions regarding route or venue or impose any other condition having regard to maintaining public order and protecting the rights of other citizens. The State only in extraordinary and exceptional W.P No.4421 of 2026 18 circumstances can restrain a person from exercising his or her right to protest on the ground of national security. It is also an obligation of the organizers of a protest and the participants to remain peaceful, unarmed and to strictly comply with the reasonable restrictions and conditions imposed by the competent authorities. (Emphasis supplied)

In another case titled as “Faiz Ahmad Cheema v. Federation of Pakistan and others” (2018 C L C 1160), it was expounded that:- 11. Judicial dicta in Pakistan generally emphasises on the need for regulation of the right to assembly. Such a view has been expounded by various judicial fora from across the globe who, whilst recognizing the right to protest in a democracy, have attached equal significance to such protests being within the contours of the law to ensure that the public does not suffer. The field cannot be left open to a group of protestors, especially in the prevalent security environment, to do as they may please sans any legal restriction. At this stage reference to the following case law on the subject would be appropriate:
In the case of Wattan Party and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others reported as PLD 2012 SC 292, the honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan held that:

"Security of person is one of the most important fundamental rights. It is inextricably linked with the security of the State. If an when a person Islamabad performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Federation act in a manner which imperils the very existence of the State a writ of prohibition nor any other appropriate written, according to the circumstances of the case could be issued against him. A petition filed by a citizen asking for the issuance of an appropriate writ cannot be declined simply because his fundamental right has not yet been infringed A narrow and pedantic interpretation may lend support to the argument that security of person is not imperilled or infringed by a mere threat to the security of the State, but actually it is otherwise. Security of person in the absence of a strong, secure and stable State would be inconceivable. It would be as imaginary as drinking water from a mirage. Therefore, fundamental right of person would stand infringed the moment something tending to imperil the security of State is done...

W.P No.4421 of 2026 19 Consent to connivance at or complicity in the infringement of security of person may not be so criminal, as an act, an omission or an attitude evincing the aforesaid attributes in the infringement of security of State. It is rather pedantic, perverse and preposterous to detach or disassociate security, solidarity and sovereignty of the State from fundamental rights.... Security of the State is like a ship. On cannot have a safe and smooth sailing into the ship by permitting others to drive a hole into that...."
In the case of D.G. Khan Cement Company Ltd. v. Federation of Pakistan and others reported as PLD 2013 Lahore 693, the honourable Lahore High Court held:

"17. Fundamental rights and their protection is essential to a modern democracy. Take human rights out of democracy, and democracy has lost its soul ... However, even in a democracy fundamental rights have limitations, this is because "in a democratic society, a human right may be limited to ensure the very existence of the state; to ensure its continued existence as a democracy; to ensure public health; to ensure public education; as well as other national causes..."
19. "Laws could restrict human rights, but only in order to make conflicting rights compatible or to protect the rights of other persons or important community interests..."

[Emphasis added] The Indian Supreme Court in its verdict reported as (2012) 5 SCC l (Ramlila Maidan. Incident, In Re) held that the freedom of speech, right to assemble and demonstrate by holding dharnas and peaceful agitations are the basic features of democratic system. The Indian Supreme Court, however, proceeded to observe that it is the abundant duty of the State to aid the exercise of the right to freedom of speech as understood in its comprehensive sense and not to throttle or frustrate exercise of such rights by exercising its executive or legislative powers and passing orders or taking action in that direction in the name of reasonable restrictions. The preventive steps should be founded on actual and prominent threat endangering public order and tranquillity, as it may disturb the social order.
In the case of Rama Muthuramalingam v. The Deputy Superintendent of Mannargudi, Tiruvarur District etc., the Madras High Court held as under:

"... It may be mentioned here that Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, which guarantees to all citizens the right to W.P No.4421 of 2026 20 freedom of speech and expression is subject to Article 19(2), which states: Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, insofar as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with Foreign States, public order, decency or morality or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

23. Thus, in conclusion, it is held that that though Respondent No.4 had the right to assemble and protest, however, that right was subject to legal restrictions which included the prerogative of the District Administration to earmark a particular place for a protest and ensure that life of the public remains unaffected. So much so, it was mandatory upon Respondent No.4 to give prior notice to the District Administration specifying the details (time, date and duration) of the proposed rally/protest and ensure that it was conducted within the parameters of the law. On the threshold of equality, the fundamental rights of a particular person/party cannot supersede the rights of the rest of the populace.”
(Emphasis supplied)

In case titled “Messrs SHAHEEN FREIGHT SERVICES through Partner and 14 others v. FEDERATION OF PAKISTAN, through Secretary, Ministry of Petroleum and NaturalResources and 3 others”(2021 C L C 323[Sindh]), it was held that:- “It is paramount to record that the right to protest is not unfettered and that it remains subject to all just restrictions, especially that such class action must be devoid of any resort to violence and / or any infraction of the law. Any attempt or perpetration of violence and / or precipitation of a law and order situation is disapproved by the law and strict sanctions are envisaged for the perpetrators. The respondent No. 3, or any entity for that matter, remains at liberty to solicit prosecution in respect of any violence or other criminal conduct directed there against to the fullest extent of the law, however, a mere apprehension of such conduct, unjustifiably attributed to individuals, cannot be sustained as justification for marginalization of the said persons in the arena of commercial enterprise.” (Emphasis supplied)

W.P No.4421 of 2026 21 23. In view of the foregoing precedents, there remains no cavil with the settled proposition that, although fundamental rights are guaranteed by the Constitution, however, such rights are not absolute or unfettered. The enjoyment of a fundamental right carries with it a corresponding obligation to exercise the same within the constitutional and legal limits prescribed for the protection of the rights and legitimate interests of others. No individual can claim a right, howsoever fundamental in character, in a manner that infringes upon, impairs, or imperils the corresponding rights and freedoms of fellow citizens. Constitutional guarantees are thus to be construed harmoniously, so as to preserve the delicate equilibrium between individual liberty and the equal entitlement of others to the protection of their own fundamental rights. The exercise of one constitutional right cannot, therefore, be permitted to operate as a licence for the infringement of another's rights, nor can the assertion of individual freedom be elevated above the constitutional order itself.

24. Now, adverting to the question of jurisdiction of this Court. The relevant constitutional provision is Article 199(1)(c), which empowers the High Court, where no other adequate remedy is provided by law and on the application of an aggrieved person, to make an order giving directions to “any person or authority, including any Government” exercising any power or performing any function “in, or in relation to” any territory within the jurisdiction of that Court, where necessary for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

25. On one extreme, learned Advocate-General, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, invites our attention to construe Article 199 as though it contained the words “within the Province in which the W.P No.4421 of 2026 22 High Court is situated” and thereby to exclude every function of a provincial government merely because the government or its officers have their ordinary seat outside Islamabad. Such an interpretation would, however, read the words “in, or in relation to” out of the Constitution. The Constitution does not provide merely that the function must be performed physically within the territory; it expressly includes a function performed “in relation to” that territory. However, Article 199(1)(c) does not confer upon a High Court a general supervisory jurisdiction over another Province. The constitutional distinction is, therefore, a High Court may issue a direction to a governmental authority outside its territorial seat where the governmental power or function sought to be regulated is itself being exercised in, or has a direct and proximate legal relation to, territory within that High Court's jurisdiction and the direction is necessary for enforcement of a fundamental right within that territory. Conversely, a High Court cannot employ Article 199(1)(c) as a roving instrument to regulate governmental functions which remain wholly internal to another Province and have no sufficiently direct constitutional nexus with the territory before the Court.

26. Under Article 199(1)(c) of the Constitution, this Court is under a bounden duty to enforce the fundamental rights of the citizens within its territory. The writ issued by this Court under Article 199(1)(c) is distinct from those issued under paragraphs (a) and (b) of clause (1) of Article 199 of the Constitution. The latter being rooted in the common law tradition. This distinction is also reflected in the plain text of paragraph (c) inasmuch as the directions under the aforesaid paragraph can be issued to W.P No.4421 of 2026 23 any person including any Government unlike paragraph (a), where the directions must remain confined to the person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Federation, a Province or a local authority. As such, the expanse of paragraph (c) is much broader than paragraph (a) or for that matter paragraph (b) of clause (1) of Article 199. It is in this context that this Court has to examine the question whether appropriate directions can be issued to the executive authorities of the Provinces or any other persons in the instant Petition. Suffice it to say, this Court is mindful that it cannot issue any directions to the executive authorities performing functions outside its territorial jurisdiction under paragraph (a) of clause (1) of Article 199 unless they transgress and act within the jurisdiction of this Court. However, and as noted above, the obligations of this Court under paragraph (c) are quite distinct. Under this paragraph, there is a positive duty imposed upon this Court to enforce fundamental rights of the persons or citizens within its territorial jurisdiction. The questions raised in the instant petition do not revolve around any present actions of the executive authorities of the Provinces which are likely to result in infringement of his fundamental rights, it is rather the likely inaction of the executive authorities of a Province or the declared political activities of some persons (which has happed at least twice in the recent past), which has triggered filing of this petition. In this backdrop, it is thus held that where any action or inaction of executive authorities or any other person, based on cogent information available on the record, results in or is likely to result in infringement of the fundamental rights of the citizens within the territorial jurisdiction of this Court, this Court shall assume jurisdiction and hold such executive W.P No.4421 of 2026 24 authorities or any other person to account for their actions or inactions.
27. In view of what has been noted above and based on the record of the recent past, this Petition is found to be maintainable on jurisdictional plain.

28. Adverting to the other merits of instant petition, the principal authority relied upon by learned counsel for the petitioner, learned Attorney-General and learned Advocate General ICT is Suo Motu Case No.7 of 2017, PLD 2019 SC 318, commonly known as the Faizabad Dharna Case. The relevant portions/paragraphs of the same have already been reproduced above. However, reiterating,in the said case, the hon’ble Supreme Court was dealing with a prolonged sit-in which had substantially paralysed Islamabad and Rawalpindi, obstructed roads, affected access to courts, hospitals and schools, disrupted business and caused damage to public and private property. The Court treated the controversy as one involving enforcement of several Fundamental Rights and, because of its public dimension, within the scope of Article 184(3) as it then stood. The governing principle of that judgment is not that protest is unlawful. Quite the contrary, the hon’ble Court recognized the constitutional character of peaceful protest. But it simultaneously made clear that the right of assembly is not absolute and remains subject to law and reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order. The Court's essential proposition may be expressed in the short phrase that the “right to assemble and protest” is protected but is circumscribed when its exercise infringes the Fundamental Rights of others. W.P No.4421 of 2026 25 29. The Hon’ble Court specifically connected the obstruction of roads and interference with ambulances, education, courts, businesses and property with Articles 9, 15, 18, 23 and other constitutional guarantees. It emphasized that the State's responsibility is not discharged by merely declaring that protesters possess a constitutional right. The State is also obliged to protect the rights of those who are not participating in the protest. Another important proposition that emerges from the judgment is that public roads are meant for public movement and cannot be converted indefinitely into camping grounds for political protest. The constitutional right of assembly cannot be interpreted as a right of perpetual occupation of infrastructure which belongs equally to all citizens. This judgment yields four propositions which are directly applicable here in this case i.e first, peaceful political assembly is constitutionally protected, second, the right is subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of public order, third, where a protest infringes the rights of other citizens, the State has a positive obligation to act and fourth, public authorities are required to prepare prospectively for foreseeable large-scale demonstrations rather than wait until irreparable consequences have occurred.

30. The matter in hand is prima facie not based on mere speculations and apprehension as the history has demonstrated the obvious conduct of the political party in disregarding not only the Court orders but also the assurances given by its leadership to remain peaceful during the assembly/sit-ins. The judgment in “Islamabad High Court Bar Association through its President Muhammad ShoaibShaheen v. Federation of Pakistan”,(PLD 2022 SC 511), is even more connected with the matter before us. In the W.P No.4421 of 2026 26 said case, the petition before the hon’ble Supreme Court arose out of the anticipated PTI march into Islamabad on 25 May 2022 and the apprehension that blockades of roads and highways would prevent ordinary citizens from performing their daily activities and exercising their right of movement under Articles 9 and 15 of the Constitution. The hon’ble Supreme Court recognized that peaceful protest enjoys constitutional protection. The core proposition was that the right cannot be denied except on lawful, reasonable and proportionate grounds. At the same time, the executive was required to ensure that the rights of the general public were not unlawfully impaired and that public and private property remained protected. However, as is obvious from the judgment, the assurances were disregarded by the then Chairman of the political party himself. For ready reference, the relevant paragraphs of the judgment are hereby reproduced:- “In a petition filed by the Islamabad High Court Bar Association under Article 184(3) of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 ("Constitution"), it was complained that in anticipation of a protest march into Islamabad by the workers of a political party on 25.05.2022, the Federal Government had blocked highways to and roads within the Capital to prevent entry and movement of the protestors. As a result the general public was prevented from conducting their daily lives contrary to the guarantees under Article 9 and Article 15 of the Constitution. As explained later, after being conveyed the assurances by the top party leadership that a peaceful assembly will take place at a specific venue in Islamabad, a learned three Member Bench directed all concerned Executive authorities to prepare the venue including providing security for the holding of the rally. Likewise, all protesting political workers were directed to disengage and remain peaceful. These directions were issued by the order of the learned Bench passed at about 6:00 p.m. on 25.05.2022.

2. Later, an application being C.M.A. No. 3447 of 2022 was filed at about 10:30 pm on 25.05.2022 by the learned Attorney General for Pakistan ("AGP"). It alleged that the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf ("PTI") leadership, in particular its Chairman Mr. Imran Khan, had contrary to his assurances given to the Court directed his party members and supporters to march into Islamabad and reach D-Chowk located in the sensitive Red Zone area of the Capital. He has read from the order of this Court passed on 25.05.2022. The Court had directed Dr.BabarAwan, Sr. ASC and Mr. Faisal Fareed, ASC appearing for the PTI leadership to seek assurance from their client that PTI workers/ supporters would remain W.P No.4421 of 2026 27 peaceful and follow the guidelines issued by the Court from time to time. That they will neither obstruct road traffic or cause damage to private/public property nor take the law into their own hands. In this respect the two learned counsel on instructions from the top leadership of PTI gave a categorical assurance that the party rally would neither block the Sirinagar Highway nor otherwise cause inconvenience to the public and citizens at large and that their rallies shall be conducted in a peaceful and lawful manner without causing any damage to public or private property.

3. In view of these commitments, the Court by its aforesaid order passed on 25.05.2022 directed the Chief Commissioner, Islamabad Capital Territory ("ICT") to provide the ground located in the area between Sectors H-9/G-9 of Islamabad for the political rally; and also directed the Inspector General of Police ("IGP"), ICT to forthwith take measures including making security arrangements to prepare the venue for holding the PTI rally. Furthermore, the Court directed that the lawyers and other persons reportedly placed under arrest in raids conducted without any complaint or FIR being recorded against them shall be released from custody forthwith. The AGP undertook that houses, offices and private premises shall neither be raided in an attempt to arrest nor shall political workers or supporters of PTI or any other political party be arrested unless an FIR was lodged against them or the commission of any heinous or cognizable offence by them was suspected. Accordingly, a direction in the said terms was issued by the Court. Finally, the Court recorded its expectation that the top leadership of all concerned political parties shall direct their workers and supporters to remain calm, disengage and not to create law and order situation under any circumstances. Equally, it was noted that the top functionaries of the Government including the Interior Ministry shall ensure that excessive or disproportionate use of force against the political workers is discontinued immediately.

4. In the foregoing background the AGP argued that having agreed to hold the PTI rally at the ground in the H-9/ G-9 area of Islamabad as recorded by the order of the Court, Mr. Imran Khan shortly thereafter instructed PTI supporters to reach D-Chowk in the Red Zone of Islamabad. To establish this retraction a video recording of Mr. Imran Khan's statement made after the passing of the above said order was played on the multimedia screen before the Court. He contended that in the above circumstances, Mr. Imran Khan appears to have invited his supporters to dishonor the assurance given on his behalf to the Court. As a result, private and public properties were damaged and destroyed. Some trees in the greenbelt of Blue Area of Islamabad were put on fire. 31 Police Officers were injured by the stones pelted by the crowd and Article 245 of the Constitution had to be invoked in the middle of the night by calling the armed forces in aid of civil power. The learned AGP accordingly requested the Court to take action against Mr. Imran Khan for breach of his assurances given to the Court.

5. Finally, the AGP informed that Mr. Imran Khan had issued a statement this morning at a location on Jinnah Avenue (leading to D-Chowk) that after witnessing the teargas shelling by the law enforcement agencies he will not proceed with the sit-in at D-Chowk. He gave six days' time to the Government to dissolve the assemblies and announce a date for elections.

6. The Court views the foregoing events with concern. It is apparent that the assurances conveyed to the Court by the learned W.P No.4421 of 2026 28 counsel for the top leadership of the PTI may have been dishonored by the workers/ supporters/ sympathizers of the party by proceeding to the D-Chowk in the Red Zone area and by allegedly committing acts of arson and destruction of public and private properties on the way. However, we note that in the early morning today Mr. Imran Khan reached Jinnah Avenue leading to D-Chowk and announced the postponement of his sit-in at Islamabad for six days. As a result, further damage to property or injury to human life has been averted. (Emphasis supplied)

In addition to above, it is pertinent to mention here that in November-2024, when members of PTI were heading to ICT, this Court passed order dated 21.11.2024 in W.P No.3597 of 2024; however, admittedly, the said order was also flouted. For ready reference, the same is hereby reproduced as under:- “Pursuant to earlier order of this Court, Minister for Interior, Secretary Interior, Government of Pakistan as well as Chief Commissioner, ICT and Inspector General of Police, ICT, Islamabad entered appearance and informed the Court that the members of a political party are heading towards Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) for protest and sitin and the respondents No.1 to 4 are making joint effort to ensure law and order situation remains normal and no disruption is caused in life of an ordinary person.

2. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that life in Islamabad Capital Territory comes to a complete halt whenever there is any political activity, protest or sit-in. It was contended that the petitioner is a trader by profession and has fundamental right of livelihood and freedom of movement as enshrined in the Constitution. It was submitted that it is the obligation of respondents No.1 to 4 to ensure that whenever there is any political activity or protest, no hindrance is caused in the fundamental rights of the petitioner or for that matter any citizens of Islamabad Capital Territory.

3. After hearing the Minister for Interior, Advocate General, ICT, Islamabad and learned counsel for the petitioner, it is clear that respondent No.5 has made an announcement to hold a political rally and sin-in in ICT on 24.11.2024. In somewhat similar circumstances, this Court, in Writ Petition No.2974/2024, vide order dated 05.10.2024, observed that fundamental rights of freedom of assembly and movement are provided to the citizens of Pakistan, however, they are subject to proportional and reasonable restrictions. It is also provided in the Constitution that such restrictions are only justifiable through legitimate purposes which must be in the best interest of the larger public. Maintenance of peace and law and order in Islamabad Capital Territory is the responsibility of the Ministry of Interior and ICT Administration and while performing their duties and functions, the principles of proportionality and legitimacy of public purpose and aim bind the said authorities to prevent harsh or disproportionate W.P No.4421 of 2026 29 restrictions which would otherwise amount to unlawful infringement of rights.

4. Keeping in view the sensitivity of the Capital of the country, the legislature recently enacted Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, 2024, whereby for an assembly in Islamabad Capital Territory, an application is to be made in writing to the District Magistrate not later than seven days of the intended assembly (Section 3 ibid). The referred application is to be processed and appropriate order is to be given regarding permission for assembly. This Court was informed that till to date, no such application has been made. This Court was also informed that the President of Belarus with his delegation of more than sixty persons is arriving on 24.11.2024 and their protection and freedom of movement is of utmost important and directly involves relationship with another country, hence the larger public interest is involved. This Court was also informed that though there is some communication with the leadership of respondent No.5 but no formal engagement as such has been made.

5. Keeping in view the freedom of movement and assembly and fundamental rights of followers of respondent No.5, they have that right which is subject to law ibid Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, 2024, it would be appropriate that respondent No.1 constitute the committee to be headed preferably by the Minister for Interior or any other person to engage with the leadership of respondent No.5, informing them of the sensitivity over the weekend due to movement of the President of a foreign country. The terms of engagement can be put forward and settled by respondent No.1. The committee so constituted shall also include the Chief Commissioner, ICT, and any other person which the Minister for Interior deems appropriate.

6. This Court is sanguine that as and when such formal engagement is made, some development would take place. In case, no breakthrough is made, then to ensure law and order situation is the responsibility of respondents No.1 to 4 without minimum disruption to the life of ordinary citizens and no violation of the Act, 2024 is committed. As the law on the subject is clear as daylight, respondent No.1 to 4 shall do the needful for ensurance of maintenance and law and order in ICT, Islamabad. In this regard, no protest or rally or for that matter sitin shall be allowed by Respondents No.1 to 4 in violation of Act of 2024.

7. Though no one is in attendance on behalf of respondent No.5, it is expected that the leadership of respondent No.5 shall take into account the factors which have been put forwarded by Minister for Interior and engage in meaningful communication with the committee so constituted. In this regard, respondents No.1 to 4 shall file a report before the next date of hearing.
(Emphasis supplied)

This Court has also taken note of order passed dated 18.03.2022 in W.P No.1077 of 2022 titled “Muhammad Asif Gujjar vs. W.P No.4421 of 2026 30 Federation of Pakistan, etc”. In said writ petition, the petitioner, a practicing Advocate and citizen of Islamabad Capital Territory, sought directions to the concerned executive authorities to prevent political assemblies/gatherings at D-Chowk/Red Zone, apprehending obstruction of public roads and infringement of citizens’ fundamental rights. This Court considered the competing constitutional guarantees of freedom of movement under Article 15 and peaceful assembly under Article 16 of the Constitution, observing that neither right could be exercised so as to unlawfully impair the other. It was held that political, religious or social gatherings must remain lawful, peaceful, without arms and subject to the restrictions imposed by law, particularly in the context of maintenance of public order. Relying upon earlier judgment in “Faiz Ahmed Cheema v. Federation of Pakistan” (2018 CLC 856) and the directions issued in W.P. No.1082 of 2022, this Court observed that regulation of assemblies and imposition of reasonable restrictions fell within the domain of the executive authorities, who were constitutionally obliged to assess the attendant risks and safeguard the fundamental rights of all citizens. The executive and law-enforcement agencies were held dutybound to protect life, liberty and freedom of movement, and to prevent any assembly threatening such rights.

31. Similarly, before this Court, in W.P. No.1026 of 2024, titled “Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaaf through Aamer Masood Mughal v. Federation of Pakistan etc., the petitioner, a political party, challenged the refusal of the respondents to grant permission for holding a public gathering, initially proposed for 23.03.2024 and subsequently rescheduled for 06.04.2024. The refusal was based, inter alia, on law-and-order and security concerns, whereas the W.P No.4421 of 2026 31 State relied upon the prevailing wave of terrorism. In the said case, this Court, while relying upon its earlier orders in Muhammad Asif Gujjar v. Federation of Pakistan etc. (W.P. No.1077/2022), Asma Malik v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Interior etc. (W.P. No.1082/2022), and Faiz Ahmed Cheema v. Federation of Pakistan through Ministry of Interior (2018 CLC 856), held that the Deputy Commissioner, Islamabad Capital Territory, is the competent authority to grant or refuse permission for a political or other gathering. While recognizing the executive’s authority to regulate assemblies in the interest of public order and security, this Court emphasized its corresponding constitutional duty to safeguard the fundamental rights of citizens.

32. However, it is a matter of regret that, notwithstanding the aforesaid orders passed by this Court, the same were not adhered to by the political party concerned, and the ensuing protests were conducted in a manner which could neither be regarded as peaceful nor reconciled with the constitutional and legal parameters governing the exercise of the right of assembly. The constitutional protection accorded to peaceful protest cannot be construed as extending to acts or conduct that disregard judicial directions, disturb public order, impede the rights and freedoms of others, or otherwise transgress the limits prescribed by law.

33. It is pertinent to mention here that during the course of arguments, this Court, with one time dispensation, allowed the C.M No.3 of 2026 filed on behalf of Deputy Commissioner/District Magistrate, Islamabad Capital Territory, under Section 151 of the CPC, read with Article 164 of the Qanun- W.P No.4421 of 2026 32 e-Shahadat Order, 1984, whereby permission to place electronic material on record and to play video clips of political party’s protests in the years 2022 and 2024 was sought. The video clips were accordingly played during the course of arguments of learned Advocate General, ICT. In the video clips the actions of protesters were highly disturbing and were reflective of violence and aggression. Most importantly, PTI was, both in May-2022 and November-2024 as also presently, in power in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. With the governmental resources of the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa at its disposal and fully used and exploited to achieve PTI’s political objectives, the administration of the ICT was unable to deal with the ensuing situation. The administration of ICT was unable to contain the unlawful assembly of persons who marched towards the ICT both in May- 2022 and in November-2024. Needless to say, when the marchers were also armed, being escorted by the police of a Province and aided by all state/governmental resources at their disposal, unless deadly clashes had occurred, it was literally impossible for the local administration of ICT to contain them. As such, the fundamental rights of the citizens within ICT could not be guaranteed. As has been discussed above, the hon’ble Supreme Court has categorically declared, in Suo Motu Case No.7 of 2018 (PLD 2019 SC 318) that any activity resulting in infringement of fundamental rights of the persons or citizens is illegal and unconstitutional. Furthermore, it is declared that aggression by a federating unit against another or against the Federation in any form or manner including, by way of any march/rally/procession is unconstitutional, illegal and unlawful. Any person, authority or Government organizing, participating or propagating in such marches/rallies/processions shall be liable to the consequences W.P No.4421 of 2026 33 provided under the law and the Constitution. The activities of said political party, in May-2022 and November-2024 in the ICT created serious security and law and order situation in the ICT. It is a matter of record that as a consequence of such activities of the PTI, public and private properties were damaged, citizens’ right to trade, business and profession was seriously hindered and obstructed, educational activities were seriously affected, and the movement of citizens residing in the ICT was restricted.

34. The material placed before us is substantially different from an entirely speculative apprehension. There are repeated public announcements of a procession towards Islamabad on 27 September 2026, including statements of the Chief Minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa that the date was firm and that he would lead the march. The proposed destination is known; the political nature of the gathering is known; its intended arrival in Islamabad is known; and the constitutional rights allegedly exposed to risk are identified. The existence of previous protests, newspaper reports, prior clashes or historical disruption may demonstrate why preventive preparation is warranted. Admittedly, till date, no application has been filed under section 3 of the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, 2024.

35. Insofar as other grounds questioning maintainability of this petition are concerned particularly those raised in view of the provisions of the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act, 2024, it is held that none of the provisions of the aforesaid Act hinder bringing this Petition to this Court. To the contrary, the provisions of the aforesaid Act have not been adhered to by the Chief Minister, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and others who have declared their W.P No.4421 of 2026 34 intention to march towards and lay siege to the ICT for purposes which are extraneous to the Constitution and the law. Therefore, instant petition is held to be maintainable, even otherwise too.

36. Learned Advocate-General, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has also objected that the Chief Minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has not been impleaded, although the entire petition proceeds on the premise that he has announced that he will lead the proposed march. In this regard, it is noted that notice to Advocate General KPK was not issued under Order XXVII-A of the CPC. He was representing the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as well as the Chief Minister, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, therefore, the objection is untenable and accordingly turned down. Even otherwise, other than, learned Advocate General, KPK, none of the learned Advocates General have raised any question on jurisdiction of this Court in issuing appropriate directions to the executive authorities of their Provinces or to any other person under Article 199 (1)(c) of the Constitution.

37. In the present case, the petitioner has gone beyond a bare political objection. He has identified himself as a businessman operating in Islamabad and has pleaded that the proposed disruption may directly interfere with movement, transportation, supply chains and the conduct of his business and thereby affect rights protected by Articles 15 and 18 of the Constitution. The Court is satisfied that the petition discloses a sufficiently concrete constitutional grievance to cross the initial threshold of standing, particularly when the event is identified by date and destination.

38. During the course of proceedings of this writ petition, the Chief Secretary as well as Inspector General of Police, Khyber W.P No.4421 of 2026 35 Pakhtunkhwa have submitted their affidavits, Mark-A and Mark- B, respectively, which have been made part of record of instant case.

39. For the foregoing reasons, instant writ petition is disposed of with the following directions and orders:i. No political party, political leader, Provincial Government or public office holder has any lawful right to occupy any public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas, buildings or other such like places within or leading to or out of the ICT, obstruct or in any manner hinder the free movement of the citizens, pursuit of trade, business or profession, access to medical facilities or educational institutions within the ICT;

ii. The Provincial Governments including, the Chief Ministers of the Provinces shall ensure that no governmental resources, public funds or officials, either directly or indirectly, shall be used, raised or participate, on any pretext, in any march/procession/rally leading towards the ICT;

iii. The Provincial Governments including, the Chief Ministers of the Provinces shall ensure that no official vehicle, machinery, or any other equipment is used to aid and/or facilitate the people participating in any march/procession/rally leading towards the ICT;

iv. The Provincial Governments including, the Chief Ministers of the Provinces shall ensure that no public servant is compelled, coerced, induced or otherwise required to participate in any march/procession/rally leading towards the ICT;

v. The administration of the ICT including, the Ministry of Interior shall ensure that no one residing within the ICT undertakes any activity which results in offending the rights of other citizens or persons guaranteed under Articles 9, 15, 18, 23, 24 and 25A of the Constitution; vi. The Chief Secretaries and Inspectors General of Police of the Provinces, the Federal Secretary Interior, the Chief Commissioner and the Inspector General of W.P No.4421 of 2026 36 Police of ICT shall forthwith, under intimation to the Registrar of this Court, issue following directions and instructions to the officials of the Federal and the Provincial Governments performing functions in the ICT or in the Provinces to the effect that:
(a) no official shall comply with any order compelling him/her to aid or facilitate any march/rally/procession leading towards the ICT;
(b) any official who is so compelled shall forthwith inform the respective Chief Secretary/Chief Commissioner or the Inspector General of Police of the respective Province or the ICT;

(c) no official shall permit any person to participate in any march/rally/procession leading towards the ICT with an intent to obstruct, or to hinder or as a consequence of which free movement, trade, business or commerce, access to educational institutions, medical facilities, peaceful and lawful use of properties in the ICT are adversely affected; (d) the Chief Secretaries of the Provinces, the Chief Commissioner of the ICT and the Inspectors General of Police shall forthwith establish a helpline or such other mode of direct access/communication as they may deem necessary to enable officials to inform them of any coercion or inducement by any person including, any political leader or public office holder, in this respect;

(e) the Chief Secretaries of the Provinces, the Chief Commissioner of the ICT and the Inspectors General of Police shall promptly take departmental action against any official who either violates this order or the directions and instructions issued by them, in this regard.

vii. Any person, whether legal or natural, who undertakes any activity which results in violation of fundamental rights of the citizens within the ICT, shall be deemed to have violated the Constitution and shall be liable for the consequences stipulated under the law;

viii. Any public office holder, who undertakes any activity which results in violation of fundamental rights of the citizens within the ICT, shall be deemed to have violated the Constitution and his/her oath of office W.P No.4421 of 2026 37 under the Constitution and shall be liable for the consequences stipulated under the Constitution and the law.
40. Foregoing are the reasons of our short order dated 14.09.2026.
